# Compiled and interpreted languages {#sec-ch-compiled}

> *"Premature optimization is the root of all evil."* — Donald Knuth
> [@knuth1974].

```{python}
from cppbook import run, show, sh, write
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- define precisely what a **compiler**, an **interpreter**, a **virtual
  machine** and a **just-in-time** (JIT) compiler are, and place C, C++,
  Python, Java and JavaScript on that spectrum;
- explain **where the time goes** when a program is interpreted, and measure
  the speed difference between Python and C++ on the same algorithm;
- state and **prove Amdahl's law**, and use it to decide whether rewriting part
  of a program in C++ is worth it;
- **prove** that the "interpret first, compile when it pays" strategy of JIT
  compilers is never worse than twice the best possible choice;
- compare the two models on **portability** (source vs binary, ABIs, data
  models), **confidentiality** (what a binary reveals) and **development
  workflow**;
- choose an execution model that fits the requirements of a project.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
The difference between interpreted and compiled languages, and how it affects
performance, portability, confidentiality and the development process.
:::

## Intuition: the simultaneous interpreter and the translated book

At an international conference, a **simultaneous interpreter** listens to the
speaker and renders each sentence as it comes: nothing has to be prepared in
advance, a correction is heard immediately, but every sentence costs the
interpreter's effort *every time it is spoken*, and the interpreter must be in
the room. A **translated book** is the opposite: translating takes time up
front, but afterwards readers read at full speed, with no translator present —
and the translation only helps readers of *that* language.

Interpreting and compiling a program are the same two strategies, applied to a
text written for people (the source code) and a "reader" that understands only
machine code (@sec-von-neumann). Every property in this chapter — speed,
portability, confidentiality, comfort of development — follows from this
picture.

## Definitions {#sec-compile-definitions}

Let us make the picture precise. Call $L$ the language of the source program
and $M$ the machine language. A program $p$ written in $L$ *means* a function
$[\![p]\!]_L$ from inputs to outputs (we ignore side effects for the moment).

::: {#def-interpreter}
## Interpreter and compiler
- An **interpreter** for $L$ is a program $\mathit{int}$ that receives a
  program $p$ *and* its input $x$ and produces the output:
  $\mathit{int}(p, x) = [\![p]\!]_L(x)$.
- A **compiler** from $L$ to $M$ is a program $\mathit{comp}$ that receives
  only $p$ and produces a program $p' = \mathit{comp}(p)$ in $M$ with the same
  meaning: $[\![p']\!]_M = [\![p]\!]_L$. The input $x$ is given later, to $p'$.
:::

*In one line:* an interpreter does the work *with* the data; a compiler does
the translation *before* the data arrives, once and for all.

The definition explains the first trade-off: the interpreter must analyse $p$
while it runs, possibly analysing the same statement millions of times inside a
loop; the compiler analyses each statement once, but nothing can run until it
has finished. It also explains the vocabulary of **times**: things that happen
in $\mathit{comp}$ happen at **compile time**, things that happen in $p'$ at
**run time**.

::: {.deep}
## The Futamura projections: a compiler is a specialised interpreter
In 1971 Yoshihiko Futamura observed that the two notions of
@def-interpreter are linked by **partial evaluation** [@futamura1999]. A
*specialiser* $\mathit{spec}$ takes a two-argument program and fixes its first
argument: $[\![\mathit{spec}(f, a)]\!](b) = [\![f]\!](a, b)$. Then:

1. $\mathit{spec}(\mathit{int}, p)$ is a program that, given $x$, computes
   $\mathit{int}(p, x) = [\![p]\!](x)$: it is a **compiled version of $p$**;
2. $\mathit{spec}(\mathit{spec}, \mathit{int})$ maps $p$ to the compiled
   version of $p$: it is a **compiler**;
3. $\mathit{spec}(\mathit{spec}, \mathit{spec})$ turns interpreters into
   compilers: a **compiler generator**.

The first projection follows directly from the definition of $\mathit{spec}$;
the second and third by applying the same definition twice and three times.
The idea is not only theoretical: GraalVM's Truffle framework and PyPy build
fast language implementations by specialising interpreters.
:::

## The spectrum of implementations {#sec-spectrum}

"Compiled language" and "interpreted language" are convenient shortcuts, but
the distinction belongs to **implementations**, not to languages: there are C
interpreters and Python compilers. Real systems sit on a spectrum:

| Strategy | How it runs | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **pure interpretation** | walk the source (or its syntax tree) and execute it | early BASICs, shell scripts |
| **bytecode + virtual machine** | compile to a compact intermediate code, then interpret it (@sec-python-language) | CPython, early Java |
| **just-in-time (JIT) compilation** | start interpreting; compile the frequently executed parts to machine code while the program runs | Java HotSpot, JavaScript V8, PyPy |
| **ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation** | compile everything to machine code before running | C, C++, Rust, Go, Fortran |

: How languages are implemented {#tbl-spectrum}

CPython is in the second row: your `.py` file is compiled to bytecode (cached
in `__pycache__/*.pyc`), and the bytecode is interpreted by a loop written in
C. C and C++ are almost always in the last row — the topic of this part. The
history of the middle rows, from Lisp and APL systems of the 1960s to modern
JITs, is surveyed by Aycock [@aycock2003].

## Where the time goes {#sec-where-time-goes}

### Measuring the gap

Take one algorithm and implement it in both languages. For every $n$ from 1 to
300 000 we count the steps of the **Collatz** process — halve $x$ if it is even,
otherwise replace it by $3x + 1$, until $x = 1$ — and add them up. It is a
good benchmark because it is pure arithmetic and branching, its running time
depends on the data (no compiler can precompute it), and nobody knows a
formula for the result (that every $n$ reaches 1 is the famous unsolved
**Collatz conjecture** [@lagarias2010]).

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output: true
import time

def collatz_total(n_max):
    """Total number of Collatz steps for all starting values 1..n_max."""
    total = 0
    for n in range(1, n_max + 1):
        x = n
        while x != 1:
            x = x // 2 if x % 2 == 0 else 3 * x + 1
            total += 1
    return total

t0 = time.perf_counter()
result = collatz_total(300_000)
t_python = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"Python (CPython): total = {result:,}   time = {t_python:.3f} s")
```

The same algorithm in C++, compiled twice: without optimisation (`-O0`) and
with optimisation (`-O2`).

```{python}
code = r"""
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    std::uint64_t total = 0;                         // 64-bit unsigned integer (@sec-ch-c-intro)
    for (std::uint64_t n = 1; n <= 300'000; ++n) {
        std::uint64_t x = n;
        while (x != 1) {
            x = (x % 2 == 0) ? x / 2 : 3 * x + 1;
            ++total;
        }
    }
    std::chrono::duration<double> elapsed = std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - start;
    std::cout << "total = " << total << "   time = " << elapsed.count() << " s\n";
}
"""
show(code, name="collatz.cpp")
write("collatz.cpp", code)
sh("g++ -std=c++20 -O0 collatz.cpp -o collatz_O0 && ./collatz_O0")
sh("g++ -std=c++20 -O2 collatz.cpp -o collatz_O2 && ./collatz_O2")
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output: true
import re, subprocess, cppbook
def cpp_time(exe):
    out = subprocess.run(["./" + exe], cwd=cppbook.BUILD, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
    return float(re.search(r"time = ([\d.e-]+)", out).group(1))
t_o0, t_o2 = cpp_time("collatz_O0"), cpp_time("collatz_O2")
print(f"speed-up of C++ -O0 over Python: {t_python / t_o0:5.1f}x")
print(f"speed-up of C++ -O2 over Python: {t_python / t_o2:5.1f}x")
```

The exact numbers depend on the machine (these were measured on the computer
that built the book), but the order of magnitude — **tens of times** — is
typical for tight loops of arithmetic.

### Why: the cost of dispatch

Look at what each implementation executes for **one** iteration of the inner
loop. CPython executes bytecode instructions; we can list those of the loop
body with `dis` (@sec-python-language):

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output: true
import dis
first = collatz_total.__code__.co_firstlineno                 # line of "def"
loop_lines = {first + 5: "while x != 1", first + 6: "x = ...", first + 7: "total += 1"}
body = [i for i in dis.get_instructions(collatz_total) if i.positions.lineno in loop_lines]
for ins in body:
    print(f"{loop_lines[ins.positions.lineno]:<13} {ins.opname:<22} {ins.argrepr}")
print(len(body), "instructions in the listing")
```

The listing shows the loop test twice (CPython 3.13 places a copy at the
bottom of the loop); one iteration executes 20 or 21 of these instructions,
depending on the branch taken. For **each** of them the interpreter loop of
CPython fetches the opcode, jumps to the code that implements it (the
**dispatch**), checks the types of the operands at run time (is `x` an `int`? a
`float`? a user object with `__mod__`?), operates on heap-allocated integer
objects of arbitrary precision, and updates reference counts. Here is the same
loop, as a C++ function, compiled with `-O2`:

```{python}
show(r"""
#include <cstdint>

std::uint64_t collatz_steps(std::uint64_t x) {
    std::uint64_t steps = 0;
    while (x != 1) {
        x = (x % 2 == 0) ? x / 2 : 3 * x + 1;
        ++steps;
    }
    return steps;
}
""", name="steps.cpp")
sh("g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -S steps.cpp -o - | sed -n '/^_Z13collatz_stepsm:/,/\\.size/p' | "
   "grep -Ev '^\\s*\\.(cfi|p2align|size)'")
```

The whole loop is a handful of register instructions: test the lowest bit
(`testb $1`, is $x$ odd?), shift right by one (`shrq`, i.e. $x/2$), compute
$3x+1$ in a single `leaq` (address arithmetic $x + 2x + 1$ reused for
arithmetic), add one to the counter, compare with 1, jump. No type checks, no
memory allocation, no dispatch: the compiler knew at compile time that `x` is
a 64-bit unsigned integer, and even replaced `% 2` and `/ 2` by bit
operations.

A simple cost model makes the comparison quantitative. If a computation
performs $N$ elementary operations, each doing useful work $w$, an AOT-compiled
program takes about $T_c \approx N w$, and an interpreter about
$T_i \approx N (w + d)$, where $d$ is the **interpretive overhead** per
operation (dispatch, type checks, boxing). The ratio
$$
\frac{T_i}{T_c} \approx 1 + \frac{d}{w}
$$
is large exactly when the operations are **cheap** ($w$ small: integer
arithmetic, comparisons) and close to 1 when they are **expensive** ($w$
large: a matrix multiplication, a database query, a network request). This is
why the gap you measure depends so much on *what* the program does, and why
Python is fast enough for most programs: its time is spent in expensive
operations implemented in C (sorting, `dict` lookups, NumPy) or waiting for
input.

## Amdahl's law: is it worth rewriting? {#sec-amdahl}

Suppose a Python program is too slow. Should we rewrite it in C++? Rewriting
everything is expensive; usually we rewrite the **hot spot** — the part where
most time is spent — and call it from Python (@sec-ch-cpp-python). How much
faster does the *whole* program become?

::: {#thm-amdahl}
## Amdahl's law
Let a program run in time $T$, and let a fraction $p \in [0, 1]$ of that time
be spent in a part that we speed up by a factor $s > 0$, leaving the rest
unchanged. The overall speed-up is
$$
S(p, s) = \frac{T}{T_{\text{new}}} = \frac{1}{(1 - p) + \dfrac{p}{s}},
$$ {#eq-amdahl}
and, however large $s$ is, $S(p,s) < \dfrac{1}{1-p}$ whenever $0 < p < 1$.
:::

*In one line:* the part you do not improve sets a ceiling — if 20% of the time
is untouched, nothing can make the program more than 5 times faster.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-amdahl
The unchanged part takes $(1-p)T$ before and after; the improved part took $pT$
and now takes $pT/s$. Hence $T_{\text{new}} = (1-p)T + pT/s$ and
$S = T / T_{\text{new}} = 1/\big((1-p) + p/s\big)$. For $0 < p < 1$ we have
$p/s > 0$, so the denominator is strictly greater than $1-p > 0$ and
$S < 1/(1-p)$. As $s \to \infty$, $p/s \to 0$ and $S \to 1/(1-p)$, so no
smaller ceiling exists. $\blacksquare$
:::

Gene Amdahl made the argument in 1967 to warn against expecting too much from
parallel computers [@amdahl1967]; his paper is in words, and the formula is the
later standard rendering of it [@hennessy2017, §1.9]. The same reasoning
applies to any partial improvement.

::: {#exm-amdahl-rewrite}
## Rewriting a hot spot
A data-processing script runs in 100 s. Profiling (measuring where the time
goes, e.g. with Python's `cProfile`) shows 70 s in a parsing loop, 30 s in
other work. Rewriting the loop in C++ makes it 40 times faster. Then
$p = 0.7$, $s = 40$ and
$$
S = \frac{1}{0.3 + 0.7/40} = \frac{1}{0.3 + 0.0175} = \frac{1}{0.3175} \approx 3.15 .
$$
The program now takes about $100/3.15 \approx 31.7$ s. Even an infinitely fast
loop would give at most $1/0.3 \approx 3.33$, i.e. 30 s: the remaining 30 s of
"other work" are now the bottleneck. Had profiling shown only 10 s in the loop
($p = 0.1$), the same rewrite would have gained less than 11%.
:::

::: {.widget}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof amdahlP = Inputs.range([0, 0.99], {step: 0.01, value: 0.7, label: "fraction p of time improved"})
amdahlCurve = {
  const out = [];
  for (let e = 0; e <= 3; e += 0.02) {           // s from 1 to 1000 on a log scale
    const s = 10 ** e;
    out.push({s, speedup: 1 / ((1 - amdahlP) + amdahlP / s)});
  }
  return out;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-amdahl
//| fig-cap: "Amdahl's law: overall speed-up as a function of the speed-up s of the improved part, for the chosen fraction p. The dashed line is the ceiling 1/(1−p)."
Plot.plot({x: {label: "speed-up s of the improved part", type: "log"}, y: {label: "overall speed-up S", domain: [1, 1 / (1 - amdahlP) * 1.1]},
  marks: [Plot.line(amdahlCurve, {x: "s", y: "speedup"}), Plot.ruleY([1 / (1 - amdahlP)], {strokeDasharray: "4,4"})]})
```
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Measure before you rewrite
Amdahl's law turns Knuth's warning into arithmetic: an optimisation is worth
exactly as much as the fraction of time it touches. **Profile first**, then
move to C++ only the parts where the time really goes.
:::

## Just-in-time compilation: when does compiling pay? {#sec-jit}

A JIT compiler has to decide, *while the program runs*, whether a function is
worth compiling. Compiling costs time $C$ now; it saves $d = a - b > 0$ on each
later execution, where $a$ is the cost of an interpreted execution and $b < a$
that of a compiled one.

::: {#prp-jit-breakeven}
## Break-even point
If a function will be executed $k$ more times, compiling it now is worthwhile
if and only if $k\,d > C$, i.e. $k > C/d$.
:::

*In one line:* compile when the total saving of the future runs exceeds the
one-off cost of compiling.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-jit-breakeven
Interpreting the $k$ runs costs $k a$; compiling first costs $C + k b$. The
second is smaller iff $C + kb < ka$, i.e. $C < k(a - b) = kd$. $\blacksquare$
:::

The difficulty is that the JIT **does not know $k$**: it cannot see the
future. A natural strategy, used in essence by real JITs with their
invocation counters, is to **interpret until the time wasted equals the cost of
compiling, then compile**. Surprisingly, this simple rule is provably close to
optimal. It is the computer-science classic known as the **ski-rental
problem** (rent skis each day, or buy them once?), analysed by Karlin, Manasse,
Rudolph and Sleator [@karlin1988].

::: {#thm-ski-rental}
## Interpret-then-compile is 2-competitive
Let $m = \lfloor C/d \rfloor$, and let the strategy THRESHOLD interpret the
first $m$ executions and compile before execution $m+1$ (if it happens). For
every number $k$ of executions, the cost of THRESHOLD is at most **twice** the
cost of the best choice made with knowledge of $k$.
:::

*In one line:* by the time THRESHOLD compiles, it has wasted at most $C$ by
interpreting — the same amount that an all-knowing strategy would have had to
pay anyway.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-ski-rental
Every execution costs at least $b$ whatever we do, so subtract $kb$ from all
costs: what remains is $d$ per interpreted execution and $C$ for compiling.
The best choice in hindsight then costs $\mathrm{OPT}' = \min(kd, C)$.

*Case $k \le m$.* THRESHOLD never compiles and pays $kd$. Since
$k \le m \le C/d$, $kd \le C$, so $\mathrm{OPT}' = kd$: THRESHOLD is optimal.

*Case $k > m$.* THRESHOLD pays $md + C \le C + C = 2C$ (because $md \le C$).
Since $k \ge m + 1 > C/d$ (by definition of the floor), $kd > C$ and
$\mathrm{OPT}' = C$. So THRESHOLD pays at most $2\,\mathrm{OPT}'$.

Adding back $kb$: $\mathrm{ALG} = \mathrm{ALG}' + kb \le 2\,\mathrm{OPT}' + kb
\le 2(\mathrm{OPT}' + kb) = 2\,\mathrm{OPT}$. $\blacksquare$
:::

No deterministic strategy can guarantee a factor below 2 by much: an adversary
who stops the program right after the strategy compiles makes it pay for both
the interpretation and the compilation [@karlin1988]. Real JITs refine the
idea with several tiers (a quick, lightly optimising compiler first, an
aggressive one for the hottest code) and with information gathered while
interpreting, such as the actual types seen — something an AOT compiler for a
dynamic language cannot know.

## Portability {#sec-portability}

**Portability** is the ability to run a program on different platforms. It
comes in two forms, and the two execution models trade one for the other.

- **Source portability**: the *source code* can be compiled or run unchanged on
  another platform. Python code is highly source-portable: it runs wherever an
  interpreter exists. Standard C and C++ are source-portable too — that is the
  purpose of the ISO standards — provided the code avoids platform-specific
  APIs and the behaviours the standard leaves to the implementation.
- **Binary portability**: the *compiled file* runs elsewhere. A compiled C++
  executable is tied to a processor **instruction set** (x86-64, ARM64, …), an
  **operating system** (the format of the file, the system calls) and an
  **ABI** (application binary interface: how arguments are passed, how objects
  are laid out, how names are mangled). Python source and bytecode have no such
  tie, which is why the *same* `.py` file runs on Windows, Linux and macOS.

The executable produced in @sec-toolchain announces its platform in its
header:

```{python}
sh("g++ -std=c++20 -O2 collatz.cpp -o collatz && file collatz | cut -d, -f1-3 && "
   "readelf -h collatz | grep -E 'Class|Machine|OS/ABI'")
```

It is a 64-bit ELF file for x86-64 Linux: Windows (which uses the PE format)
cannot load it, and a Mac with an ARM processor cannot execute its
instructions. To support three platforms, you build three executables — on
three machines, or with a **cross-compiler**, which runs on one platform and
generates code for another.

### Implementation-defined behaviour: the data models

Even *source* portability of C and C++ has traps, because the standards leave
some choices to the implementation. The best-known is the **size of the integer
types** (@sec-ch-c-intro): the standard only guarantees minimum ranges, and
64-bit platforms made different choices:

| Data model | `int` | `long` | `long long` | pointer | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ILP32 | 32 | 32 | 64 | 32 | 32-bit Linux and Windows |
| LP64 | 32 | **64** | 64 | 64 | 64-bit Linux, macOS, other Unix systems |
| LLP64 | 32 | **32** | 64 | 64 | 64-bit Windows |

: Sizes in bits of the integer types in common data models {#tbl-data-models}

A program that stores a file size or a pointer in a `long` works on 64-bit
Linux and silently truncates on 64-bit Windows. The portable fix is to say what
you mean: the fixed-width types of `<cstdint>` (`std::int64_t`) and the types
made for the job (`std::size_t` for sizes, @sec-ch-c-intro).

::: {.callout-note}
## Python inherits the problem one level down
Pure Python code is portable, but packages with compiled extensions (NumPy,
PyTorch) must be built separately for each platform and Python version: this is
why PyPI distributes many **wheels** for one release of such a package, one per
platform tag (@sec-ch-pip).
:::

## Confidentiality {#sec-confidentiality}

When you give someone a Python program, you give them the **source**: they can
read it, change it and copy its ideas. Bytecode files (`.pyc`) are not much
better, because bytecode keeps names, constants and structure:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output: true
import dis

def check_licence(key):
    SECRET = "ACME-1234-XYZ"                 # an embedded "secret"
    return key == SECRET

code = check_licence.__code__                # what a .pyc file stores (marshalled)
print("names:", code.co_varnames, "| constants:", code.co_consts)
```

A compiled executable distributes machine code, which is much harder to read:
variable names, comments and the structure of the source are gone. That is a
real advantage when the algorithm is a trade secret. But compilation is
**not encryption**. Text constants, the names of external functions, and —
unless stripped — the names of your own functions survive in the binary:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

bool check_licence(const std::string& key) {
    static const char secret[] = "ACME-1234-XYZ";    // an embedded "secret"
    return key == secret;
}

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    std::cout << (argc > 1 && check_licence(argv[1]) ? "licence ok\n" : "invalid licence\n");
}
""", name="licence.cpp", args=("WRONG-KEY",))
sh("strings licence | grep -i acme; nm -C licence | grep check_licence; "
   "strip licence && echo 'after strip:' && (nm licence 2>&1 | head -1); strings licence | grep -i acme")
```

`strings` prints every run of printable characters in a file: the "secret" is
there in plain text, before and after `strip` (which removes the symbol table
with function names, but not data). An optimising compiler sometimes splits a
short constant into the operands of a few instructions, so that `strings` sees
only fragments — a disassembler reassembles it in a minute. And with a **decompiler** such as Ghidra,
released as open source by the US National Security Agency, an analyst can
reconstruct readable pseudo-code of `check_licence` from the machine code.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Never put secrets in a program you distribute
Passwords, API keys and licence-checking logic shipped inside an executable
must be assumed **readable** by anyone who has the file. Compiling gives
*obscurity*, not security. This is Kerckhoffs's principle, formulated in 1883
for military ciphers [@kerckhoffs1883]: a system must stay secure even if
everything about it except the key falls into the enemy's hands. Secrets
belong on a server you control, or in configuration supplied by the user.
:::

## The development workflow {#sec-dev-workflow}

The two models also feel different to work with:

| | Interpreted (Python) | Compiled (C++) |
|---|---|---|
| edit → see the result | immediate; a REPL allows experiments line by line | an extra build step: seconds to minutes in large projects |
| type errors | found when the line runs (maybe in production) | most found at compile time, before running |
| performance tuning | limited; move hot spots to compiled code | fine control over memory layout and machine code |
| debugging | tracebacks with names and values; `pdb` | debugger and sanitizers (@sec-debugging); some errors are silent (undefined behaviour) |
| distribution | ship sources + dependencies; the user needs an interpreter | ship one executable per platform; no interpreter needed |

: Development workflow in the two models {#tbl-workflow}

Neither column wins everywhere, which is why so much real software — and almost
all AI software — is **hybrid**: the program logic, experiments and glue are
written in Python, and the expensive kernels (linear algebra, tensor
operations, data loading) in C, C++ or CUDA, called from Python. NumPy and
PyTorch are built this way (@sec-crash-courses). Making a Python program and a
C++ program cooperate is the subject of @sec-ch-cpp-python.

## Choosing an execution model {#sec-choosing-model}

The four criteria of this chapter give a checklist.

| If the project needs… | Prefer |
|---|---|
| maximum speed on cheap, repeated operations (simulation, signal processing, games, numerical kernels) | AOT compilation: C, C++, Rust |
| fast iteration, exploration, data analysis, glue between systems | an interpreted language: Python |
| a single file to install on users' machines, with no runtime to install | a compiled executable per platform |
| one artefact that runs everywhere a runtime exists | Python source, or a bytecode VM (JVM) |
| to keep the algorithm away from casual readers | compiled code (but never rely on it for secrets) |
| both speed in a few places and productivity elsewhere | a hybrid: Python + compiled extension or helper process |

: A decision checklist {#tbl-choose-model}

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** The CRM of @sec-ch-project-crm is written in C++ because
the brief asks for it (R1, @sec-crm-brief), and this chapter tells us what we
gain and what we do not. Performance is **not** the reason: with a few thousand
customers every operation takes microseconds in any language (@sec-amdahl:
there is no hot spot worth optimising). The real advantages are a **single
native executable** that an agency can run without installing an interpreter,
and a strongly typed code base in which many mistakes are caught at compile
time. The price is **binary portability**: the README must explain how to build
the program on each platform (R12), and the code must avoid
implementation-defined assumptions such as the size of `long`
(@tbl-data-models).
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **"Python is slow, so rewrite everything in C++."** Amdahl's law: only the
  fraction of time you speed up matters. Profile first.
- **"C++ is always fast."** Unoptimised builds (`-O0`), poor algorithms or
  needless copies can make C++ slower than good Python calling NumPy.
- **Benchmarking a debug build**, or a loop whose result is never used (the
  optimiser may delete it entirely). Print or otherwise use the result.
- **Assuming binary portability.** An executable built on Linux does not run on
  Windows or on another processor; ship one build per platform.
- **Assuming type sizes**: `long` is 64 bits on Linux and 32 on Windows. Use
  `<cstdint>` types when the size matters.
- **Hiding secrets in compiled code.** `strings` finds them in seconds.
:::

## Summary

- An **interpreter** computes $[\![p]\!](x)$ from $p$ and $x$ together; a
  **compiler** translates $p$ into an equivalent machine program before $x$ is
  known. Real implementations sit on a spectrum: pure interpretation, bytecode
  + VM (CPython), JIT (Java, JavaScript, PyPy), AOT (C, C++).
- Interpretation adds an overhead $d$ per elementary operation (dispatch, type
  checks), so the slowdown $\approx 1 + d/w$ is large for cheap operations — tens
  of times on our Collatz benchmark — and small for expensive ones.
- **Amdahl's law**: speeding up a fraction $p$ of the time by $s$ gives
  $S = 1/((1-p) + p/s) < 1/(1-p)$. Profile before optimising.
- A JIT that interprets until the wasted time equals the compilation cost is
  **2-competitive** (ski rental).
- Compiled code is **source-portable** (with care about implementation-defined
  sizes) but **not binary-portable**; it hides the source but **not** its
  secrets; it moves many errors to compile time at the price of a build step.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-cpp2-amdahl}
A training pipeline spends 60% of its time loading and decoding images and 40%
in the model. (a) What is the overall speed-up if decoding becomes 10 times
faster? (b) And if instead the model becomes 10 times faster? (c) What is the
best possible speed-up obtainable by optimising only the decoding?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) $p = 0.6$, $s = 10$: $S = 1/(0.4 + 0.06) = 1/0.46 \approx 2.17$.
(b) $p = 0.4$: $S = 1/(0.6 + 0.04) = 1/0.64 \approx 1.56$.
(c) $1/(1-0.6) = 2.5$. Improving the larger fraction helps more, but even an
infinitely fast decoder leaves the model's 40%.
:::

::: {#exr-cpp2-inverse}
Invert Amdahl's law: you need an overall speed-up of $S = 2$ and the part you
can optimise takes $p = 0.75$ of the time. What speed-up $s$ must that part
reach? Is $S = 4$ achievable?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
From $1/S = (1-p) + p/s$: $p/s = 1/S - (1-p) = 0.5 - 0.25 = 0.25$, so
$s = 0.75/0.25 = 3$. For $S = 4$: $1/4 - 0.25 = 0$, so $s$ would have to be
infinite: $S = 4 = 1/(1-p)$ is exactly the ceiling of @thm-amdahl, which no
finite $s$ reaches.
:::

::: {#exr-cpp2-jit}
A function costs 50 µs per interpreted call and 2 µs per compiled call;
compiling it costs 12 ms. (a) After how many calls does compiling pay off?
(b) With THRESHOLD (@thm-ski-rental), what is the worst ratio between its cost
and the optimum if the function is called exactly 251 times?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) $d = 48$ µs, $C = 12\,000$ µs: compiling pays when $k > C/d = 250$ calls.
(b) $m = \lfloor 250 \rfloor = 250$; with $k = 251$, THRESHOLD interprets 250
calls ($250 \cdot 50 = 12\,500$ µs), compiles (12 000 µs) and runs one compiled
call (2 µs): 24 502 µs. The optimum is $\min(251\cdot 50,\ 12\,000 + 251\cdot 2)
= \min(12\,550,\ 12\,502) = 12\,502$ µs. Ratio $\approx 1.96 \le 2$, as the
theorem guarantees: this $k$ is close to the worst case.
:::

::: {#exr-cpp2-portable}
Which of these lines are portable between 64-bit Linux and 64-bit Windows, and
how would you fix the others? (a) `long bytes = file_size;` where the file can
exceed 4 GiB; (b) `int count = v.size();` for a `std::vector v`;
(c) `std::int64_t bytes = file_size;`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) Not portable: `long` is 32 bits on Windows (LLP64), so sizes above
$2^{31}-1$ bytes overflow. Use `std::int64_t` or `std::uintmax_t`. (b) Compiles
everywhere, but `size()` returns `std::size_t` (64 bits on both platforms), so
a vector with more than $2^{31}-1$ elements would not fit in `int`; use
`std::size_t` (or `auto`). (c) Portable: the width is fixed by the type.
:::

::: {#exr-cpp2-measure}
Rerun the Collatz benchmark of @sec-where-time-goes with `n_max` equal to
1 000 000 in both languages, and also with PyPy if you can install it. Does the
ratio stay the same? Explain with the cost model $1 + d/w$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
The ratio between CPython and C++ stays roughly constant, because both times
grow in proportion to the number of elementary operations $N$; the ratio
$T_i/T_c \approx 1 + d/w$ does not depend on $N$. PyPy, a JIT, typically lands
between the two: its compiled loops remove most of the dispatch overhead $d$
once they are "hot" (@sec-jit), but keep some checks that C++ does not need.
:::

## Further reading {.unnumbered}

- @aho2006, ch. 1 — compilers and interpreters, the phases of a compiler; the
  standard textbook on the subject ("the Dragon Book").
- @aycock2003 — a short history of just-in-time compilation, from the 1960s to
  Java.
- @amdahl1967 — the original three-page argument; @hennessy2017, §1.9 — the
  formula and its use in computer architecture.
- @karlin1988 — competitive analysis and the ski-rental argument.
- @futamura1999 — the reprint of Futamura's 1971 paper on partial evaluation.
- @bryant2016, ch. 5 — how to measure and optimise program performance on real
  hardware.
- @kerckhoffs1883 — the principle that a system's security must not rest on the
  secrecy of its design.
